stem: Invented for practice. A toy passes marks A, B and C at steady beats. The marks have equal gaps. Mark its next place and say what repeats.
answer: One equal gap beyond C; equal gaps at equal beats.
steps: One equal gap beyond C. | Cite the repeating gap.
samples: One equal gap beyond C, because each beat covers the same gap. | The next mark stays at C.

stem: Watch the marble and cup. What changes do you notice? What possible cause should we test?
answer: Describe visible cup travel or sound; suggest a tentative cause.
steps: Separate what was observed from a possible cause. | Accept plausible ideas without energy words.
samples: The cup went farther; maybe approach speed mattered. | My guess proves every result.

stem: Record one observation from the rolls. Add one question for another trial.
answer: An observed change and a repeatable question, kept distinct.
steps: Observation describes something seen. | Question could be checked by another trial.
samples: The cup moved. Will a repeated faster roll move it farther? | I observed what tomorrow will do.

stem: The pictures show two train speeds. Draw your possible explanation for the tower's different changes. Add one question that could test your idea.
answer: Tentatively connect train motion to displaced pieces; ask a testable question.
steps: Drawing gives a plausible tentative connection. | Question proposes an observable test, such as repeated rolls. | Do not require energy vocabulary; accept labels or a scribe to distinguish language access from understanding.
samples: Faster motion may scatter more pieces; repeat both speeds to check. | My guess proves every future result.

stem: A child says, "The next cup roll will go farther." Label this as observed or expected.
answer: Expected; that future trial has not happened.
steps: Label expected. | Distinguish future prediction from observation.
samples: Expected; it has not happened. | Observed; the child said it.

stem: Two setups use the same marble and surface. Setup A changes speed and cup size. Setup B changes only speed. Cross out the extra change.
answer: Cup size in A; B isolates speed.
steps: Cross out cup size. | Either speed or cup size could cause the result in A.
samples: Keep cup size fixed to isolate speed. | Changing both makes it fairer.

stem: Watch the repeated marble rolls. Record whether the comparison stayed fair. Note any extra change and one observed effect.
answer: Honestly record conditions and effects, including accidental changes.
steps: Check marble, cup, surface, cup start and contact alignment. | Record a visible effect; no invented measurement.
samples: The same cup start was kept; one off-center hit needs flagging. | Different cups prove speed matters.

stem: A ring rolls into a lid. Plan a fair test of faster and slower ring rolls. Show what changes, what stays, and what you watch.
answer: Change speed; keep ring, lid, surface, lid start and contact arrangement fixed. Repeat both speeds and observe lid motion.
steps: Vary speed only. | Keep ring, lid, surface, target start and contact fixed. | Observe lid motion and repeat both speeds. | Accept concise notes or labeled drawing; a language gap is not a control error.
samples: Change speed; keep the ring, lid, surface, start and contact fixed. Repeat and watch travel. | Use a different lid for each speed.

stem: A slower roll uses one cup. A faster roll uses a larger cup. Cross out the change that hides the speed effect.
answer: Cross out larger cup; keep the receiver unchanged.
steps: Identify cup change. | Retain the same cup for both speeds.
samples: Use the same cup to isolate speed. | Keep changing cups.

stem: Invented for practice. A pencil starts at ruler mark 2 and ends at 7 centimeters. Show its travel by counting intervals.
answer: Five one-centimeter intervals; travel is 5 centimeters.
steps: Count intervals 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, 5 to 6 and 6 to 7. | Record 5 centimeters, not endpoint 7.
samples: Five intervals, so 5 centimeters. | The pencil travels 7 centimeters.

stem: Invented for practice. A ribbon is 5 centimeters long. Place one mark for its length on a labeled line plot.
answer: One mark above 5, axis labeled length in centimeters.
steps: Use equal whole-centimeter intervals. | Place one mark at 5; label length in centimeters.
samples: One mark at 5 on a length-in-centimeters axis. | The axis measures energy in centimeters.

stem: Record each cup trial in the table. Give speed, trial label and travel in centimeters. Keep unreadable trials visible.
answer: Six trial rows with units and honest unclear readings.
steps: Each row has speed and trial label. | Nearest whole-centimeter mark; less than one centimeter is not zero. | Repeat an unclear reading once; keep both entries.
samples: S1: 3 centimeters; S2: unreadable; S2 repeat: 4 centimeters; other trials retained. | Erase the awkward result and invent a matching one.

stem: The washer starts at 6 centimeters and stops at 15 centimeters. Another trial moves it 9 centimeters. Record both travel distances with units. Plot both trials on a labeled line plot.
answer: 9 centimeters twice; two stacked marks at 9, axis labeled distance in centimeters.
steps: 15 minus 6 gives 9 centimeters. | Second travel is 9 centimeters. | Two marks above 9 on a distance-in-centimeters axis. | Allow enlarged axes or a scribe for motor and language access.
samples: 9 centimeters and 9 centimeters; two marks at 9 on a labeled distance axis. | First travel is 15 centimeters.

stem: Review the pencil record from day 3. Count the spaces from 2 to 7 centimeters. Label what the ruler measures.
answer: 5 centimeters of distance.
steps: Count five intervals. | Label distance in centimeters.
samples: Five centimeters of travel. | The endpoint 7 is the travel.

stem: Choose one row from our cup table. Add its mark to the class plot. Label one observed cup change.
answer: Match the row to its mark; describe observed cup motion.
steps: Match distance and speed series. | Keep equal intervals and speed labels. | Describe an effect, never energy units.
samples: The S1 mark matches its row; cup motion changed after contact. | The cup moved centimeters of energy.

stem: What happens repeatedly after our faster marble rolls? What might that tell us about the moving marble?
answer: If controlled repeats separate consistently, greater effects support more motion energy in the faster marble.
steps: Check actual records first. | Repeated greater controlled effects support more motion energy. | Overlap calls for further trials, not altered records.
samples: Each faster effect is farther, supporting more motion energy. | The same marble has equal energy at both speeds.

stem: The same disk hits the same target. What repeated pattern connects its speed and motion energy? Use both displays.
answer: Both displays show each faster trial moving the target farther; faster disk motion has more energy.
steps: Table and plot: slower 2, 3, 2; faster 7, 8, 7 centimeters. | Every faster effect exceeds every slower effect. | Connect speed to more motion energy. | Accept concise labels or a scribe for language access.
samples: Both displays show every faster trial farther; faster motion has more energy. | The same disk has equal energy at both speeds.

stem: Review our marble record. Point to the repeated speed difference and label what centimeters measure.
answer: Each faster effect is farther in the separating record; centimeters measure travel.
steps: Use repeats at both speeds. | Distinguish distance from energy. | Same object can have different motion energy.
samples: All faster effects are farther; centimeters label travel. | Same marble means equal energy.

stem: Use our marble observations to explain aloud why cup motion supports your claim. Point to repeated evidence.
answer: Faster marble motion has more energy available to pass to the cup; repeated greater effects support this.
steps: Claim about the same marble at two speeds. | Repeated controlled effects as evidence. | Energy passes at contact and changes cup motion; distance is not energy units.
samples: Faster marble motion has more energy. Repeated faster rolls move the cup farther. Energy passes to the cup at contact. That changes motion and supports the claim. | Fast means fast; evidence is unnecessary.

stem: Write three short evidence notes: repeated outcomes, a fixed condition, and what the cup did.
answer: Three relevant notes, not a complete written explanation.
steps: Name repeated outcomes. | Name a fixed condition. | Describe cup motion without energy units.
samples: All faster effects farther; same cup start; cup moved after contact. | The cup traveled centimeters of energy.

stem: Use trial evidence to explain how target motion supports the speed-energy relationship.
answer: Faster cylinder motion has more energy; all three faster effects exceed all three slower effects; transfer changes target motion.
steps: Identify faster roll. | Cite repeats at both speeds. | Explain energy passing to the target, changing its motion; greater controlled effects support more available energy. | Allow a scribe for the independent child's own explanation.
samples: The faster roll has more motion energy. Every faster effect is farther. Energy passes to the target at contact and changes its motion. Greater controlled effects support more available energy. | Same cylinder means equal energy.

stem: Review day 5's marble record. Point to the repeated effects supporting more motion energy at faster speed.
answer: Use separating outcomes at both speeds, conditions fixed.
steps: Cite repeated effects at both speeds. | Same object does not imply equal energy when speed differs.
samples: All faster effects were farther in this record. | One marble always has equal motion energy.

stem: Invented for practice: the same toy tire hits the same index card. Each speed has three trials. Every faster trial moves the card farther. Choose the explanation using transfer.
answer: Statement A connects energy passing to the card with its changed motion.
steps: A: Faster tire motion has more energy available to transfer at contact; that changes card motion. | B: Faster tire motion has more energy because that is what faster means. | A supplies a mechanism; B restates the claim.
samples: A connects transfer to card motion, supported by repeated greater effects. | B supplies evidence by repeating faster.

stem: Match evidence strips to complete statements. Mark which observation supports the speed claim. Add a short evidence note.
answer: Greater repeated faster effects support the speed claim; fixed conditions support comparability; motion after contact supports transfer.
steps: Match independently first. | Repeated outcomes support the speed claim. | Fixed conditions support fairness, not energy quantity. | Keep the note brief; do not rewrite an explanation.
samples: Every faster trial farther supports the claim; same tire supports fairness. | Same tire proves equal energy.

stem: Strengthen this explanation with trial evidence and a transfer reason.
answer: Add repeated greater tube motion and energy passing from hoop to tube, changing tube motion.
steps: Cite repeated farther tube motion at faster speed. | Explain transfer at contact changing tube motion. | Link controlled greater effects to more available motion energy, never energy units of distance. | Allow a scribe for the child's own independent explanation.
samples: Repeated faster rolls moved the same tube farther. Energy passed to the tube, changing its motion. Greater controlled effects support more available energy. | The same hoop always has equal energy.

stem: Review day 6 feedback and the earlier marble record. Label what centimeters measure. Explain aloud why the same marble can have different motion energy.
answer: Centimeters measure travel. Faster motion of the same marble has more energy, supported by repeated greater effects.
steps: Label distance, not energy. | Compare repeated controlled effects at both speeds. | Faster motion has more energy available to transfer.
samples: Centimeters measure travel. Faster motion of the same marble has more energy, supported by repeated greater effects. | The same marble always has equal motion energy. (error A).

stem: Invented for practice. A resting crate has equal opposite horizontal pushes. Compare this with a stronger rightward push. Describe the arrows and motion change.
answer: Equal opposite arrows cancel; no horizontal motion change. A stronger rightward push gives an unbalanced pair and rightward motion change.
steps: Review: arrows start on the crate and point with each push. | Equal opposite pushes are balanced and cancel. | With a stronger rightward push, motion changes rightward.
samples: Equal opposite arrows cancel; no horizontal motion change. A stronger rightward push gives an unbalanced pair and rightward motion change. | The push arrow leaves the crate and carries energy into air. (error J).

stem: A car moving right touches a still block. Point to the push on the block. Show a different arrow for energy passing to block motion.
answer: The force arrow starts on the block at contact and points right. An energy arrow connects car motion energy to block motion energy.
steps: Review force arrow on receiver, pointing right. | Contact means objects touch. | Destination means where transferred energy goes. | Connect car motion energy to block motion energy with a labeled energy arrow. | Arrow length does not measure energy here.
samples: The force arrow starts on the block at contact and points right. An energy arrow connects car motion energy to block motion energy. | The force arrow carries energy away into the air. (error J).

stem: Sort questions A and B as testable or needing detail. Underline the observable outcome, if given.
answer: A needs an observable outcome. B is testable; underline how far the block moves.
steps: A leaves best undefined. | B compares speeds and names block travel; keep car, block, surface, start and alignment fixed.
samples: A needs an observable outcome. B is testable; underline how far the block moves. | A is ready because best tells us what to measure. (error F).

stem: Before the roll, predict the block motion aloud. Afterward, record what each object did. Keep your observation separate from your prediction.
answer: Predict possible block motion, then honestly record car and block changes, including unclear observations.
steps: Predict before watching. | Record both motions after contact. | Mark unclear when speed or change cannot be distinguished. | Fallback C is invented, never measured.
samples: Predict possible block motion, then honestly record car and block changes, including unclear observations. | My prediction counts as something already observed. (error I).

stem: A rubber ball rolls toward an empty carton. Ask a testable question comparing two ball speeds. Predict both objects' motion and draw the push on the carton.
answer: For example: Will a faster ball move the same carton farther? Predict ball slowing and carton starting. Draw a rightward contact-force arrow starting on the carton.
steps: Question varies speed and names an observable outcome. | Prediction addresses both objects with a defensible contact explanation. | Arrow starts on carton at contact, pointing right in supplied picture. | Accept other physically defensible predictions with reasons, including rebound; not all energy must leave the ball.
samples: For example: Will a faster ball move the same carton farther? Predict ball slowing and carton starting. Draw a rightward contact-force arrow starting on the carton. | Which speed is best? (error F).

stem: Use yesterday's car and block. Choose an observable outcome for comparing speeds. Point to the push receiver and name one energy destination.
answer: Compare block travel with the same setup. Push receiver is block; block motion receives energy.
steps: Name observable block travel. | Put push on block at contact. | Energy passes to block motion; slowing is not disappearance.
samples: Compare block travel with the same setup. Push receiver is block; block motion receives energy. | Which speed is best needs no further detail. (error F).

stem: Record each collision in order. Describe both objects before and after contact. Keep unclear rows and accidental changes visible.
answer: Six honest event notes identify approach speed, both motion changes and unclear or changed conditions.
steps: Use same car, block, surface, start and alignment. | Observe actual approach speed. | Note both motions separately. | Keep unclear entries; separate invented fallback events.
samples: Six honest event notes identify approach speed, both motion changes and unclear or changed conditions. | Record the prediction as the observed result. (error I).

stem: Point to observations that support or challenge your spoken prediction. Add a short evidence note beside your original record.
answer: Identify an actual observation; retain original marks and add an evidence note in a second color or with an added symbol.
steps: Review grade 3 revision: keep original observations and initials. | Compare prediction to what happened. | Update oral expectation; name energy passing to block motion when supported.
samples: Identify an actual observation; retain original marks and add an evidence note in a second color or with an added symbol. | Erase the observation to match the prediction. (error I).

stem: Your prediction said the can would keep moving unchanged. New pictures show it slowing and the cork starting to move. Revise your prediction and energy model using these observations.
answer: A repeat can slow the can and start cork motion. Energy passes from can motion to cork motion at contact; both observations support revision.
steps: Change unchanged-motion prediction using both observations. | Revise model to connect can motion energy to cork motion energy. | Keep some can motion energy because it slows without necessarily stopping. | Accept labels and arrows or equivalent explanations.
samples: A repeat can slow the can and start cork motion. Energy passes from can motion to cork motion at contact; both observations support revision. | The can slows because its energy disappears. (error C).

stem: Use a car record from day 8. Mark one observed change and name its energy destination. Keep tomorrow's expected result separate.
answer: Identify an actual motion change; block motion receives energy. Future results are expected, not observed.
steps: Read actual record. | Follow energy to block motion. | Expectation is not observation.
samples: Identify an actual motion change; block motion receives energy. Future results are expected, not observed. | The next roll is already observed because I predicted it. (error I).

stem: Invented for practice. A practice listener reports an unclear contact sound. Show how to enter this event without calling it quiet.
answer: Add one event tick; label approach speed unknown and sound unclear. Leave motion unknown unless supplied.
steps: Tick means event, not loudness. | Write unclear sound and unknown for unsupplied speed or motion. | Never invent readings.
samples: Add one event tick; label approach speed unknown and sound unclear. Leave motion unknown unless supplied. | My expected quiet sound counts as observed sound. (error I).

stem: Log each contact in order with one tick. Add approach speed, sound report and both motion changes. Keep unclear reports visible.
answer: Six chronological entries with honest speed, sound and both motion observations; unclear retained, no numerical sound levels.
steps: Same safe listening place. | One tick per event, separate from quiet/loud/unclear report. | Both motions; invented C separate from live records.
samples: Six chronological entries with honest speed, sound and both motion observations; unclear retained, no numerical sound levels. | Sound receives all energy, so block motion needs no record. (error D).

stem: Point to one sound event and its motion notes. Explain aloud why listening alone cannot describe every energy destination.
answer: Block motion is another destination. Sound and motion observations together support transfer; sound is not an energy meter.
steps: Use a recorded event. | Include block motion and sound. | Review: same car faster has more motion energy; unclear sound cannot establish a pattern.
samples: Block motion is another destination. Sound and motion observations together support transfer; sound is not an energy meter. | All energy became sound. (error D).

stem: The same wheel hits the same box. Record sound tallies for each speed. Explain what sound and box motion suggest about energy.
answer: Slower: three quiet, zero loud. Faster: zero quiet, three loud. Repeated greater sound and motion support more starting motion energy at faster speed, transferred to motion and sound.
steps: Record three quiet slower events and three loud faster events. | Link repeated sound and motion differences to more starting motion energy in faster wheel. | Include transfer to box motion and sound. | Sound is not a total-energy measurement.
samples: Slower: three quiet, zero loud. Faster: zero quiet, three loud. Repeated greater sound and motion support more starting motion energy at faster speed, transferred to motion and sound. | The same wheel has equal starting motion energy at both speeds. (error A).

stem: Use one day 9 sound event and its motion notes. Name a destination besides sound. Compare the same car's motion energy at two speeds.
answer: Block motion is another destination. The same car has more motion energy at faster speed, supported by repeated controlled effects.
steps: Keep receiver motion alongside sound. | Review same-object speed-energy relationship. | Use repeated records; sound is not an energy meter.
samples: Block motion is another destination. The same car has more motion energy at faster speed, supported by repeated controlled effects. | All collision energy became sound. (error D).

stem: Read the scientific account beside one motion and sound record. Point to what was observed and what the account adds.
answer: Motion and sound come from observations or labeled reports. Slight warming comes from the account, not measured temperatures.
steps: Identify information sources. | Collisions can warm objects and surrounding air. | Our records contain no temperatures; no reading does not prove no warming.
samples: Motion and sound come from observations or labeled reports. Slight warming comes from the account, not measured temperatures. | We did not feel warmth, so warming cannot happen. (error E).

stem: Attach destination labels to the class energy arrows. Put each label beside its information source.
answer: Block motion and sound attach to observation or observer report; slight warming to account. Keep remaining car motion energy.
steps: Connect initial motion energy to destinations, without equal-size claims. | Motion and sound use records. | Warming uses account, not a measured temperature.
samples: Block motion and sound attach to observation or observer report; slight warming to account. Keep remaining car motion energy. | Energy disappears when the car slows. (error C).

stem: Sort labels A, B and C under observation or scientific account. Point to the record or account that supports each choice.
answer: A and B: observation or observer report. C: scientific account; no class temperature measurement establishes warming.
steps: A block motion: observed record. | B contact sound: heard or observer report. | C slight warming: scientific account. | Account does not replace unclear observations.
samples: A and B: observation or observer report. C: scientific account; no class temperature measurement establishes warming. | Warming is impossible because hands did not detect it. (error E).

stem: Revise the sphere's before-and-after energy drawing using the observations and background card.
answer: Before: sphere motion energy. After: remaining sphere motion energy plus energy transferred to cone motion, sound and slight warming. Mark motion/sound observed, warming from account.
steps: Keep initial motion energy and remaining sphere motion energy as it slows. | Add cone motion, sound and slight warming destinations. | Distinguish observations from account-based warming. | Arrows are transfers, not force or equal energy shares.
samples: Before: sphere motion energy. After: remaining sphere motion energy plus energy transferred to cone motion, sound and slight warming. Mark motion/sound observed, warming from account. | Energy disappeared when the sphere slowed. (error C).

stem: Use day 10 feedback. Point to motion evidence and the account about warming. Name a destination besides sound.
answer: Block motion is observed; slight warming comes from the account. Motion, sound and warming are destinations, not disappearing energy.
steps: Identify record and account separately. | Keep motion beside sound. | No felt warmth does not prove no warming; no temperature was measured.
samples: Block motion is observed; slight warming comes from the account. Motion, sound and warming are destinations, not disappearing energy. | All energy became sound (error D).

stem: Record each car trial, including the missing slower trial. Note both motions and any unclear observation.
answer: Record approach speed and both motion changes honestly. Retain unreadable entries; mark fallback records invented.
steps: Keep car, block, surface, block start and contact fixed. | Use observed approach speed, not force lines. | Repeat an unclear trial once if time allows; otherwise use C separately.
samples: Invented C, slower trial: the car slows and the block moves a little. I could not read the live trial, so I kept it marked unclear. | My expected result is an observation (error I).

stem: Choose one observation. Note which class question it could help answer.
answer: A specific recorded motion observation is linked to a relevant question; it is evidence, not proof of every future result.
steps: Point to an actual trial. | Connect to motion after contact or whether slower and faster effects differ. | Keep the note brief, without an integrated prediction and explanation.
samples: My slower trial showed the car slowing and the block moving a little. It helps answer whether the block moves after contact. | A prediction proves what happened (error I).

stem: Ask a testable follow-up question and predict a slower repeat. Explain how the recorded effects support the speed-energy link.
answer: Will another slower wagon roll move the carton less than a faster roll? Predict the wagon slows and the carton moves less than in faster trials. Repeated controlled greater effects support more starting motion energy at faster speed, available to transfer at contact.
steps: Question varies speed and names an observable effect. | Predict wagon slowing and less carton motion than faster trials, conditions fixed. | Explain repeated greater effects as evidence of more motion energy available to transfer. | Energy passes to destinations; it does not vanish. Accept equivalent questions, concise labels or child-directed scribing.
samples: Will another slower wagon roll move the carton less than a faster roll? Predict the wagon slows and the carton moves less than in faster trials. Repeated controlled greater effects support more starting motion energy at faster speed, available to transfer at contact. | Which speed is best? (error F).

stem: Use the car observations from day 11. Choose an observable outcome for a speed question. Name what receives energy when the car slows.
answer: Choose block movement as an observable outcome; a faster version of the same car has more motion energy. Energy reaches block motion, sound and slight warming, rather than vanishing.
steps: Name observable block motion for error F. | Review same-car speed contrast for error A. | Follow destinations for error C; warming comes from the scientific account.
samples: Choose block movement as an observable outcome; a faster version of the same car has more motion energy. Energy reaches block motion, sound and slight warming, rather than vanishing. | Which speed is best? (error F).

stem: Point to each correct overlay. Say whether it shows a push on an object or an energy destination.
answer: Overlay A shows forces on the two objects at contact. Overlay B connects truck motion energy to block motion, remaining truck motion, sound and slight warming.
steps: A: truck push arrow starts on block, points right; block push arrow starts on truck, points left. | B: arrows connect initial motion energy to named destinations, not travel paths. | No lengths or equal shares are inferred.
samples: Overlay A shows forces on the two objects at contact. Overlay B connects truck motion energy to block motion, remaining truck motion, sound and slight warming. | A push arrow carries energy into air (error J).

stem: Sort each label under push on object or energy destination. Use the correct overlays to check each choice.
answer: Push on object: truck pushes block right; block pushes truck left. Energy destination: block motion; remaining truck motion; sound; slight warming.
steps: Keep the two object pushes together. | Keep the four energy destinations together. | A force is on an object; energy arrows show where energy goes. | Accept pointing or label letters; no paragraph drafting.
samples: Push on object: truck pushes block right; block pushes truck left. Energy destination: block motion; remaining truck motion; sound; slight warming. | Sound receives all energy (error D).

stem: A bead slows after striking a card. Its model says energy vanished. Its push arrow points from the card into air. Repair this model with labels that distinguish energy arrows from force arrows.
answer: Keep remaining bead motion energy and add transfer to card motion, sound and slight warming. A force arrow starts on the object being pushed at contact, pointing in the push direction. Energy arrows connect initial energy to destinations; they are not force arrows into air.
steps: Replace vanished energy with card motion, remaining bead motion, sound and slight warming. | Force arrows show pushes on objects at contact, with correct object and direction. | Energy arrows connect initial motion energy to destinations. | Accept labeled drawing or equivalent explanation; a scribe records only child choices.
samples: Keep remaining bead motion energy and add transfer to card motion, sound and slight warming. A force arrow starts on the object being pushed at contact, pointing in the push direction. Energy arrows connect initial energy to destinations; they are not force arrows into air. | Energy vanished as the bead slowed (error C).

stem: Use day 12 feedback. Point to a push on an object. Name an energy destination.
answer: The push acts on the block or truck at contact; energy reaches receiver motion, remaining mover motion, sound and slight warming.
steps: For error J, identify the pushed object and direction. | For error C, trace energy to destinations instead of vanishing. | Warming is account-based.
samples: The push acts on the block or truck at contact; energy reaches receiver motion, remaining mover motion, sound and slight warming. | A force arrow carries energy into air (error J).

stem: Which anchor question can our records answer now? Attach a record detail or account line to that answer.
answer: Controlled repeated greater cup motion supports more starting motion energy in the faster marble. Energy passes at contact, changing both motions; sound is observed and slight warming comes from the account.
steps: Check actual repeated records before choosing an answer. | Link faster marble motion to more energy available to transfer, supported by greater controlled effects. | Keep remaining marble motion and receiving cup motion, sound and slight warming. | Label observation or account. Retain questions not settled by these sources; do not force a pattern from overlapping trials.
samples: Faster marble trials moved the cup farther repeatedly. That supports more starting motion energy available to transfer. Our listening record supports sound; the account supports slight warming. | Same marble means equal starting energy (error A).

stem: Invented for practice. A paper ball rolls toward a still paper tube. Give a conditional motion prediction for their single contact.
answer: If the ball reaches and strikes the tube, the tube may move and the ball may slow, stop or rebound. Energy can pass to tube motion.
steps: State the contact condition. | Predict physically possible changes in both objects. | One receiver only; no chain or record-explanation packet.
samples: If the ball reaches and strikes the tube, the tube may move and the ball may slow, stop or rebound. Energy can pass to tube motion. | The ball slows because energy vanishes (error C).

stem: Explain the repeated bottle results using our energy model. Predict the bottles' motions and energy destinations if the first bottle reaches the second.
answer: Every faster orange trial moves the first bottle farther and sounds louder, supporting more initial motion energy at faster speed. The orange slows as energy passes at contact. If the first bottle reaches the second, it can transfer energy to second-bottle motion and may slow, stop or rebound. Energy also reaches sound and slight warming; some may remain in moving objects.
steps: Use repeated controlled effects to connect faster orange motion with more motion energy. | Conditional second contact can start second-bottle motion and change first-bottle motion. | Include remaining motion, sound and slight warming; no disappearance or equal shares. | Warming is from the account, not a temperature measurement. Accept defensible uncertainty about reaching or moving the second bottle.
samples: Every faster orange trial moves the first bottle farther and sounds louder, supporting more initial motion energy at faster speed. The orange slows as energy passes at contact. If the first bottle reaches the second, it can transfer energy to second-bottle motion and may slow, stop or rebound. Energy also reaches sound and slight warming; some may remain in moving objects. | The same orange has equal initial motion energy at both speeds (error A).

stem: The same spool hits the same hanging flap. Explain how these repeated results connect speed and energy. Explain why flap movement supports your idea.
answer: The faster spool has more motion energy. Every faster flap travel, 11, 12 and 11 centimeters, exceeds every slower travel, 4, 5 and 4 centimeters. Energy passes at contact and changes flap motion. Repeated greater controlled effects support more energy available to transfer; centimeters measure movement, not energy.
steps: Record four separate categorical look-fors: same-spool faster motion has more energy; repeated evidence from both speed sets; energy transfer at contact changes flap motion; greater controlled movement supports more available transfer. | Accept a comparison of all trials without listing every number. | Do not infer energy quantities from centimeters. Accept labels, drawings or a scribe for language access; score the science supplied by the child.
samples: The faster spool has more motion energy. Every faster flap travel, 11, 12 and 11 centimeters, exceeds every slower travel, 4, 5 and 4 centimeters. Energy passes at contact and changes flap motion. Repeated greater controlled effects support more energy available to transfer; centimeters measure movement, not energy. | Same spool means equal starting energy (error A).

stem: Ask a testable question about speed and energy transfer in this setup. Predict a slower repeat with a before-and-after energy drawing. Use the records and background card.
answer: Will a slower roll make the same flap swing less? A repeat slower than the recorded faster rolls should usually give less flap motion and quieter sound with conditions fixed. The spool slows as energy passes into flap motion. The drawing retains remaining spool motion and connects starting motion energy to flap motion, sound and slight warming of objects and air.
steps: Record six categorical look-fors: question varies speed; question names observable transfer outcome; prediction includes both objects changing motion energy; prediction uses the supplied evidence; model includes sound; model includes slight warming of objects and air from background. | Accept equivalent questions and defensible sound uncertainty. | Slowing does not require stopping; retain remaining spool motion. | Force arrows are not energy paths into air. Warming is account-based, not measured here. | Scribing records the child response without coaching.
samples: Will a slower roll make the same flap swing less? A repeat slower than the recorded faster rolls should usually give less flap motion and quieter sound with conditions fixed. The spool slows as energy passes into flap motion. The drawing retains remaining spool motion and connects starting motion energy to flap motion, sound and slight warming of objects and air. | All energy vanishes when the spool slows (error C).

stem: Use the anchor records. Match a repeated effect to the speed claim. Label what centimeters measure.
answer: Repeated controlled greater cup effects support more motion energy in the faster marble. Centimeters measure travel, not energy.
steps: Use retained anchor evidence, not a fresh assessment table. | Compare repeated effects at both speeds. | Name travel as the measured quantity.
samples: Repeated controlled greater cup effects support more motion energy in the faster marble. Centimeters measure travel, not energy. | Centimeters measure energy (error B).

stem: Use the anchor model. Point to a destination besides sound. Keep remaining motion when an object still moves.
answer: Cup motion and slight warming are destinations besides sound. Some energy remains in marble motion when the marble still moves.
